opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the cleanest way to put it is that Nested Learning isn't meant to replace deep learning so much as to reinterpret what deep learning has been doing all along.

When we look at a standard deep network, we tend to think of it as one thing: a stack of layers with parameters, trained by an optimizer. The architecture is over here, the optimizer is over there, and we treat them as separate design choices. What Nested Learning suggests is that this separation is somewhat artificial. If you look closely, a model is really a collection of nested, interconnected optimization problems, each with its own context flow and its own update frequency.

Take something as basic as gradient descent with momentum. You can view the momentum term as a small associative memory that is itself being optimized: it's learning to compress the history of gradients. So the optimizer is already a learning module. Similarly, attention can be understood as an associative memory mapping keys to values, solving its own inner optimization over the tokens in context. Once you see these components through that lens, the line between "architecture" and "optimizer" starts to blur. They're all learning processes, just operating at different levels and different timescales.

So the relationship, in my view, is this: deep learning, as we practice it today, is a kind of flattened projection of a richer structure. When we stack layers, we're adding depth in one dimension, but we're mostly keeping everything at roughly two update frequencies: very fast, in-context computation and very slow pretraining updates. Nested Learning says there's another axis of depth, which is levels of learning, where different components update at different rates and compress different kinds of context.

That matters because a lot of the limitations we see in current models, especially around continual learning, fit nicely into this picture. A pretrained transformer is a bit like a patient with anterograde amnesia. It has long-term knowledge from pretraining and a short-term working memory in its context window, but nothing in between that lets new experience consolidate into lasting knowledge. The brain, by contrast, has a whole spectrum of oscillation frequencies and consolidation processes. Nested Learning is partly an attempt to bring that kind of multi-timescale structure into our models. That's what we explore with ideas like the continuum memory system and the Hope architecture.

So I'd frame it as a generalization and a new perspective rather than a break. Existing deep learning is a special case, and by making the nested structure explicit, we get a design space we weren't really exploring before: more expressive optimizers, self-modifying modules, and memory systems that sit between "frozen weights" and "context window."

r001.rationale: The response describes attention as an associative memory that maps keys to values and performs an inner optimization, but does not identify it as a non-parametric solution to a regression problem.

r002.rationale: The response contrasts Nested Learning’s view of components as learning processes with conventional separation of architecture and optimizer, but does not state that conventional deep learning views components only by their final solutions.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, Nested Learning isn't a replacement for deep learning so much as a different lens on what deep learning has been doing all along. The core observation is that a lot of things we usually treat as separate components, the architecture, the optimizer, the training loop, are actually all instances of the same thing: an associative memory that is being updated by some form of optimization, just at different time scales.

So if you look at backpropagation with gradient descent, that's one level. The weights are a memory that compresses the gradient signal from the data. But then if you look at something like Adam or momentum, the momentum term itself is a memory. It's storing a compressed summary of past gradients, and it's updated with its own little learning rule. And if you look inside a transformer, attention over the context window is also an associative memory, one that gets written at every token rather than every training step. Nested Learning says: let's stop pretending these are different kinds of objects and instead treat the whole system as a set of nested optimization problems, each with its own context flow and its own update frequency.

Once you adopt that view, two things happen. First, a lot of existing methods fall out as special cases. Linear attention, recurrent state-space models, test-time training, even the choice of optimizer, these become points in one design space rather than disconnected tricks. Second, and this is the part I find exciting, the framework suggests things that were hard to see before. If an optimizer is just a memory with a learning rule, you can ask whether it should be a deeper memory, or whether it should have more expressive update rules. If the model has levels operating at different frequencies, you can ask how to build in more levels, so there's a continuum between fast in-context adaptation and slow pretraining, instead of the hard wall we have today where the model is frozen after training.

That's really the motivation. Current models have a kind of anterograde amnesia. They learned a huge amount in pretraining, and they can hold things briefly in context, but there's nothing in between, no mechanism for consolidating new experience into longer-term parameters during use. The brain clearly has multiple timescales of plasticity, and Nested Learning is an attempt to give models that same structure in a principled way, rather than bolting on another module. So I'd say the relationship is: it's deep learning, but with the levels made explicit, and with the claim that depth in the sense of stacking layers is not the only kind of depth that matters. Depth across optimization levels and time scales matters too, and that's a dimension we've barely started exploring.

astra-6.text:
I think of Nested Learning as a way to understand and extend deep learning. It’s not necessarily a replacement. The central idea is that a learning system can contain multiple learning processes, operating at different timescales, with each process having its own objective and its own way of updating state.

Typically, we separate the architecture from the optimizer: the architecture is the model, and the optimizer is how we train it. But the optimizer also maintains state—it accumulates information from gradients and uses that information to determine future updates. From this perspective, both are parts of a larger learning system.

So instead of looking only at a sequence of layers, we look at nested learning processes: what information each process receives, what it retains, and how frequently it updates. Existing deep learning fits within that picture. The opportunity is to use that perspective to design systems that learn and retain information across more timescales, rather than treating learning as something that happens only during a separate training phase.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of Nested Learning as a way to understand and extend deep learning. Typically, we separate the architecture from the algorithm that trains it. You have a neural network, and then you have an optimizer updating its weights. In Nested Learning, we look at both as learning processes, each with its own state, its own context, and potentially its own update frequency.

That gives you a different way to think about memory. Some parts of a system change very quickly, while others accumulate knowledge much more slowly. Instead of treating learning during training and adaptation during inference as completely separate things, we can ask how these processes fit into a hierarchy of updates.

So it’s not about throwing away deep learning. It’s about making those learning processes explicit and using that perspective to design systems that can keep adapting without constantly overwriting what they already know.
